title: Plane Loses Power at Night: Wisconsin Congressman Swims From Sinking Aircraft to Safety
summary:
The plane was approaching Wausau Downtown Airport when the engine lost power. Within minutes, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and his pilot were in the water.

Tiffany, a Wisconsin Republican, was returning from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner late Saturday when the single-engine, four-seat Beechcraft Bonanza lost power. The pilot, Leonard Boltz, made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau just before 9 p.m., according to the Marathon County Sheriff's Office.

"After landing, we called 911," Tiffany wrote on X. "As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat."

A fire department airboat — a flat-bottomed vessel designed to travel over water and ice — reached the men just after 9 p.m. Both were taken to a nearby hospital, treated for minor injuries and released. Tiffany suffered a cut above his right eye that required stitches, his campaign said.

The plane remained in the lake. A no-wake buoy was placed near it, and boaters were asked to avoid the area until it can be removed. A Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson said the agency will investigate. The National Transportation Safety Board said it is waiting for the FAA to assess whether the damage was substantial enough for it to get involved.

Tiffany is running for governor of Wisconsin on the Republican ticket and has been endorsed by President Donald Trump. His Democratic opponent, David Crowley, wished Tiffany a "quick recovery" in a post on X and praised "the heroism of the pilot."

Emergency landings on water are rare and dangerous: aircraft often flip or sink quickly, and cold water can incapacitate people within minutes. In this case, both men were able to exit the aircraft and reach shallow water before help arrived.
why_it_matters: Private flying is how most non-airline flights happen, and its accident rate is far higher than that of commercial airlines — so how the FAA and NTSB investigate cases like this shapes the safety rules that affect thousands of pilots and passengers each year.

background_read: Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District is one of the largest districts east of the Mississippi River, covering a wide stretch of the state's rural north and centre; Tom Tiffany (a Republican who has represented it in the U.S. House of Representatives since 2020) was flying home from a local party dinner when the plane went down.

Wausau is a city in central Wisconsin where the Wisconsin River widens into Lake Wausau, and the Downtown Airport sits close to the water — part of why an engine failure at low altitude left the pilot little choice but to land on the lake.

Small private planes like the Beechcraft Bonanza fly the great majority of U.S. flight operations, and general aviation has a much higher rate of fatal accidents per flight hour than commercial airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration (the body that writes aviation safety rules) investigates crashes, while the National Transportation Safety Board (an independent agency) takes over the most serious ones.

Ditching a plane in water is rare and risky: aircraft often flip or sink quickly, and cold water can rob a person of the ability to swim within minutes. David Crowley (the Milwaukee County Executive and the Democratic candidate for governor) wished Tiffany a quick recovery.

perspectives.description: They highlight a calm emergency landing, a fast 911 call and an airboat crew that reached the men within minutes. Both men walked away with minor injuries, and a political rival publicly praised the pilot's heroism.

They point out that single-engine night flights over cold water carry serious risk, and that survival was far from guaranteed. In their view the crash is a reminder to ask harder questions about training, aircraft maintenance and when such flights should be avoided.

For the FAA and NTSB this is a technical puzzle: engine failure can come from fuel, mechanical or pilot factors, and only an investigation can say which. Their split of duties — the FAA assesses, the NTSB decides whether to take over — is itself part of the story.

The wrecked plane still sits in Lake Wausau, so salvage, boater safety and possible environmental concerns come next. Politically, Tiffany continues his campaign for governor with a personal survival story — and with investigators yet to explain why the engine failed.
